title: AI scams in Georgia and South Florida: How scammers use deepfakes to steal millions

reading.body:
Scammers are using deepfake technology to impersonate real people, including immigration attorneys, in fraud schemes targeting vulnerable populations. The impersonation occurs entirely outside any system designed or controlled by AI developers. In one reported case, a South Florida immigration attorney's voice and identity were cloned to deceive immigrants seeking legal services. In another, a couple lost approximately $800,000 in a cryptocurrency scam after being contacted by what they believed was a trusted individual. The attacks work because deepfakes can sound and look sufficiently authentic to bypass the natural skepticism victims might otherwise apply to unexpected contact.

These frauds exploit the gap between what a person claims to be and what verification would reveal. To catch such schemes before losses accumulate, victims would need to verify urgent requests through independent contact information, avoid sending money based on a single phone call or message, and establish separate authentication methods with people they trust. The scams are not a failure of AI deployment in a legitimate service. They are a misuse of AI technology by criminals operating outside any system that could be redesigned or monitored. It is not established whether the deepfake generation itself involved failures by AI companies, or only reflects how openly available the technology has become.

summary:
Scammers are increasingly using artificial intelligence technology to commit fraud by creating deepfakes of voices, photos, and phone calls that sound and look authentic. In Georgia and South Florida, criminals have targeted victims through various schemes, including a Cobb County couple who lost approximately $800,000 in a cryptocurrency scam and a South Florida immigration attorney whose voice and identity were cloned to deceive immigrants. According to the FBI's 2025 Internet Crime Report, Americans reported nearly $893 million in AI-enabled scam losses last year, with Florida reporting 350 AI-related complaints totaling $39.9 million and Georgia reporting 71 complaints totaling $10.4 million in losses.

Scammers use generative AI to enhance traditional fraud schemes by cloning voices from social media, spoofing phone numbers, creating fake photos, and researching personal relationships to make their requests seem legitimate. Romance and confidence scams resulted in over $19 million in losses nationwide, while voice-cloning distress scams accounted for more than $5 million. Financial institutions are warning customers to verify urgent requests directly, avoid sending money based solely on phone calls, and monitor accounts closely. Officials recommend establishing code words with family members and emphasize that verification rather than speed provides the strongest defense against these evolving scams.
